hints: Focus on what the two solutions have in common and what is different, both have $\text{Cl}^-$ and water, so the key must be $\text{NH}_4^+$ versus $\text{Na}^+$.
Remember that $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ is a sparingly soluble base, so think about what type of reagent normally dissolves a hydroxide.
Consider how $\text{NH}_4^+$ can act as an acid to remove $\text{OH}^-$ as water and pull the solubility equilibrium to the right, while $\text{Na}^+$ cannot.
walkthrough:
**Recall why magnesium hydroxide is insoluble**

Magnesium hydroxide is a sparingly soluble base. It sits in equilibrium with its ions in water.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$\text{Mg(OH)}_2(s) \rightleftharpoons \text{Mg}^{2+}(aq) + 2\text{OH}^-(aq)$$

**Compare the two cations**

Both solutions contain $\text{Cl}^-$, so chloride is not the cause. $\text{Na}^+$ is the conjugate of a strong base and is neutral in water, it cannot react with $\text{OH}^-$.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$\text{Na}^+(aq) + \text{OH}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{no reaction}$$

**Spot the acidic behaviour of ammonium**

$\text{NH}_4^+$ is the conjugate acid of the weak base ammonia, so it can donate a proton to hydroxide to make ammonia and water. Removing $\text{OH}^-$ shifts the equilibrium in Step 1 to the right, so the solid dissolves.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$\text{NH}_4^+(aq) + \text{OH}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{NH}_3(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$

**Write the overall dissolving reaction**

Putting the two equilibria together gives the full dissolving equation. Sodium chloride cannot do this, so no dissolving occurs.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$\text{Mg(OH)}_2(s) + 2\text{NH}_4^+(aq) \rightarrow \text{Mg}^{2+}(aq) + 2\text{NH}_3(aq) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$

options.A: Ionic size does not control whether a hydroxide dissolves. Dissolving here is a chemical acid-base reaction, not a size-matching or lattice substitution effect.
options.B: Both $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$ and $\text{NaCl}$ are soluble ionic salts and dissociate essentially fully in water. A difference in dissociation cannot explain the very different dissolving behaviour.
options.C: It is true that $\text{Na}^+$ and $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ are both isoelectronic with neon (10 electrons), but this fact is irrelevant to solubility in this case. It gives no mechanism for removing $\text{OH}^-$.
options.D: This is correct. $\text{NH}_4^+$ acts as a weak acid and donates a proton to $\text{OH}^-$ from $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$, forming $\text{NH}_3$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$. This removes $\text{OH}^-$ and drives the $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ equilibrium to dissolve.
